value.text: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week.The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan.Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event.For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area.“I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment,” the resident said during Monday’s meeting.Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding.Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week’s flooding.President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period.“If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn’t matter,” said Cassens. “We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can’t manage water in the quantities that we got.”District officials also discussed maintenance of waterways and ditches, including concerns surrounding a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.The district said engineering could be examined as part of developing a long-range plan.Conditions improve at Save the ChimpsSave the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding.WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater.When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved.“A short 40 hours after that, we’re almost completely dry on our roads,” said Mark Yohannan.The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary.West Fort Pierce farmer raises concernsThe concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods.Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting.Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure.“I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there’s really no right answer except for stop building,” Akerley said.Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events.Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families.“I’ve got friends that have calves dying that are flooded, they can’t get out,” he said. “It’s a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There’s people that have lost their homes.”He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage.“Just please reconsider because it’s not a good situation for everybody, and it’s only gonna get worse,” Akerley said.Officials consider what comes nextDuring Monday’s Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city’s stormwater infrastructure.Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029.He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.Meanwhile, the North St. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan.For residents and farmers still recovering from last week’s flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event?This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A dog that arrived at Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control spinning in circles in his kennel is now headed toward a future in police work.The dog, named Bayblade, caught attention for the very energy that made him stand out at the shelter."He had a tendency to spin, which is typically something that dogs will do when they are really backed up with energy and they need something to do," Arielle Weinberger said. Weinberger is a PR specialist with Palm Beach County Animal Care & Control.That energy caught the attention of animal rescue advocate Jim Bradley."I work with all sorts of rescues. Malinois, Dutch Shepherd Rescue, so a lot of local rescues. Oftentimes they might have a more challenging dog," Bradley said.He put Bayblade to the test, looking at his energy, focus and drive to work."A working dog they are genetically just a complete different dog. Their energy, their drive, their tenacity, their desire to bite and grip into whole things," Bradley said.He recognized those traits could make Bayblade ideal for police work. So Bradley contacted a canine organization in Ohio, and Bayblade was accepted."They'll be doing some bite work because he'll be a dual purpose canine that he can do apprehensions and also find find drugs or weapons," Bradley said.Now, Bayblade is getting a chance to put all that energy to work."That cute little puppy with the pointy ears that in 6 months you've got a working dog who needs to work, who needs to move, who needs to do his what he was bred to do. And so I'm happy that Bayblade is going to get that chance," Bradley said.From providing video of the dog in the kennel to the flight to Ohio, several people were instrumental in getting Bayblade — who is now called Blade — to his destination. Those involved included Fabienne with the Canine Enrichment Team, Alpha Pack K9 training, plane owners Harrison Gevirtz and Adam Young, and Wendy Cristantiello.

The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway.Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad.Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7."At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff.However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County.Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward.WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

Emergency management officials are working to assess damage and assist residents in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties and the Treasure Coast following last week’s severe flooding caused by heavy rain. In Palm Beach County, much of the water has receded, but some neighborhoods are still dealing with the aftermath. In Palm Beach County, a state of local emergency has been extended for another week. In Riviera Beach’s Long Pines Estates, piles of debris from damaged homes are stacked along the streets. Jeffrey Simms, a 14-year resident, described the impact. "The rain came, we thought it was going to stop, but it didn't. I mean, it didn't stop until it demolished our home, as you can see; this is our junk pile, which used to be our home on the inside," Simms said. Simms and his neighbor Denise Smith said they do not believe their homes were in a FEMA-designated flood zone. "It's been a devastating experience, and now my neighbors and I are left with the task of replacing everything, restoring everything, and most of us, although we have homeowners' insurance, we don't have flood insurance. Because this is not a flood zone? This is not a flood zone; it's not a flood zone," Smith said. Lucie County, officials reported receiving 273 submissions to their damage assessment survey as of Monday morning. At the height of the flooding, more than 100 roads were closed, and as of Sunday afternoon, two roads remained closed. FLOODING UPDATE: Martin County crews begin process of pumping water from flooded Hyline Drive In Okeechobee County, damage assessment teams have surveyed about half the area, with preliminary damage estimates already exceeding $10 million. Officials reported two homes destroyed and 59 others sustaining major damage. Residential losses are estimated at more than $6 million, while damage to county infrastructure is estimated at $4.3 million. The county noted that infrastructure damage alone exceeds the threshold for FEMA assistance consideration, though officials emphasized that these estimates are preliminary and could increase as assessments continue. In Martin County, officials say 30 homes have been classified as destroyed, and another 40 sustained moderate damage. A damage assessment also found an estimated $750,000 in damage to unpaved roads across the county. Martin County’s Flood Recovery Assistance webpage has been updated with additional information and resources, including details about a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) opening Tuesday, Nov. 10, as well as opportunities for community members to support neighbors in need through United Way of Martin County’s Disaster Donor Program. Some residents impacted by the flooding are still looking for relief. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I will say Riviera Beach has been out here helping us. But the biggest resource now is really funding so that we can try to get our lives back to some sense of normalcy," Smith said. "And also, for the school district, that they would reinstate my personal days that I have had to use." To assist residents, a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) will open on Tuesday, November 10, at the Wells Recreation Center in Riviera Beach. The center will operate from 7 a.m. and will be staffed by personnel from state and local agencies, as well as nonprofit organizations, to provide resources to those affected by the flooding. It's expected to run for 14 days. Participating organizations include the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Florida Department of Children and Families, Palm Beach County Office of Emergency Management, American Red Cross, and others. Martin County’s Flood Recovery Assistance webpage has been updated with additional information and resources, including details about a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) opening Tuesday, Nov. 10, as well as opportunities for community members to support neighbors in need through United Way of Martin County’s Disaster Donor program. Emergency management officials in Indian River County said the residential damage assessments are closer to being finished. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

A fire heavily damaged India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach, but firefighters prevented the flames from spreading to neighboring businesses, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.Crews responded to reports of a commercial fire on Royal Palm Beach Boulevard, just north of Southern Boulevard.Watch video of the fire:When firefighters arrived, they found the restaurant heavily involved in flames. PBCFR said a large fire was visible from the front of the building, while thick, dark smoke billowed from the rear.It took firefighters about 30 minutes to bring the fire under control.“An aggressive attack prevented the fire from going to neighboring businesses or running along the overhead space,” Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said in a statement.Adjacent businesses experienced some smoke intrusion, according to PBCFR, but no injuries were reported.India Grill and Bar sustained considerable fire damage.PBCFR fire investigators remained at the scene throughout the night as they worked to determine where and how the fire started.“The fire remains under investigation,” Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said.

Federal investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres earlier this month.The National Transportation Safety Board said in a Monday evening post on X that investigators found the cockpit voice recorder, commonly known as a CVR, at the site of the plane's initial impact.PREVIOUS REPORT: NTSB completes most on-scene work related to crash The recorder has been sent to the NTSB's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where it is being evaluated.Cockpit voice recorders can provide investigators with information about sounds and conversations inside an aircraft’s cockpit leading up to a crash.The NTSB also announced that excavation work at the initial impact site has been completed.The Learjet 60 crashed near Greenacres on Nov. 1.The NTSB did not provide additional details about what may have been captured on the recorder or when information from its examination could become available.The agency said Sunday that it had completed most of its on-scene investigative work.The investigation into the crash remains ongoing.

Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

Since 2019, the Keiser University football team has made the NAIA football playoffs each season, including making it to the title game the last four years, but that streak could be in jeopardy."We always talk about process over results, and I know the results have shown us going to countless amount of national championships but we continue to focus on the process of what got us there," said head coach Myles Russ.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Keiser's push to national prominence is thanks to an all-in approach by every man on the team, and for the last few years the leader of that attack was Shea Spencer, the former quarterback who led Keiser to two straight national title appearances.These days, however, a new signal caller, JT Tabora, has taken over."It's been awesome being the quarterback here at Keiser. I've been backup for the past two years, and it's been great learning behind him, and giving me the opportunity to start this year has been great," said Tabora.In seven games this season, the sophomore has passed for 1,300 yards and 13 touchdowns.While his numbers are strong, the Seahawks find themselves in uncharted waters. They're 6-3 and ranked 15th overall in the country, and after suffering a loss Saturday, the fellas could fall out of the top 15.Sounds like no problem, right? Well, only the top 15 teams are guaranteed a spot in the NAIA Playoffs, making Saturday's season finale against Warner a must-win."I think we can clean up some things, that's our mindset: just clean up some things, and once we get those things (fixed), we’re a tough team to beat," Tabora said.

A Palm Beach County School District employee was arrested after police said he had sexually explicit conversations with an undercover detective posing as a 14-year-old boy.Boynton Beach police said Donald Rush, 65, of Lake Worth was arrested following an investigation by the department's Human Exploitation Task Force.According to police, detectives posed as a 14-year-old boy advertising lawn mowing services on Craigslist's Community messaging board.Investigators said they were contacted by someone using the screen name "Palm Guy," who was later identified by police as Rush.Police said Rush asked the person his age, whether adult men had approached him about sexual activity and whether he had told his parents about those interactions.The conversation later moved to text messages, according to police. Detectives said they again made clear that the person Rush was communicating with was supposedly 14 years old.Despite the stated age, police allege Rush continued the conversation, asking sexually explicit questions and making statements about his own sexual activity.With assistance from the Palm Beach County School Board Police Department, detectives located and interviewed Rush. Boynton Beach police said Rush admitted his involvement during that interview.Police said Rush also claimed during the investigation that he was a youth pastor. The department did not identify a church or organization with which he was allegedly affiliated.Rush faces charges of solicitation of a minor to engage in sexual conduct and unlawful use of a two-way communications device, according to police. He was being held at the Palm Beach County Jail.Police identified Rush as an employee of the Palm Beach County School District. However, the department did not specify his position with the district.Investigators said they believe there could be additional victims.Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Rush or has information about similar incidents involving him is asked to contact Boynton Beach police Detective Joseph at 561-742-6158.

Historic flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as displaced residents wait to learn whether federal assistance will be made available.The flooding has left damage across WPTV's five-county viewing area, stretching from Indian River County through Palm Beach County.But in Martin County's Jensen Beach community, the latest numbers show just how destructive the flooding has been.Jensen Beach residents describe unlivable conditions.Michael Drawdy is among the Jensen Beach residents dealing with severe flooding inside his home."Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house," Drawdy told WPTV.Drawdy and his neighbors now face conditions they say have made their homes unlivable.Residents also told WPTV much of their immediate help has come from one another, along with churches and community donations."All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way," resident Suzie Keith said. "No one else has really helped us. I mean, we've all been helping ourselves."Florida has formally requested federal disaster assistance to help communities recover from recent flooding across Central and South Florida.At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request seeking federal assistance for communities impacted by the flooding.The request comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in portions of the state, leaving communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later."We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover," the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X.A Major Disaster Declaration must receive federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available.The state's announcement did not specify which counties are included in the request or detail what types of federal assistance Florida is seeking.The request is the latest step in the recovery process as residents, businesses and local governments continue assessing damage from the flooding.Residents say they can't afford to waitThat process comes as some Jensen Beach residents say they are already out of their homes and struggling to figure out what comes next.Keith said residents understand the process takes time but need assistance now."They know it's moving slowly and we're all out of our homes and we have nowhere to live, but they said they're doing everything they can to expedite it to FEMA," Keith told WPTV.For residents facing destroyed homes and potentially lengthy recoveries, the question is now how quickly additional assistance can reach the people who need it.Until then, Keith said neighbors are continuing to rely heavily on one another.

More than a week after a deadly Learjet crash forced businesses to close along Military Trail near Greenacres, signs of recovery are starting to emerge.On Sunday, the National Transportation Safety Board said they have begun to wrap up its on-scene investigative work.WATCH REPORT BELOW: $250K grant program for businesses proposed after Learjet crashPalm Beach County is now proposing a $250,000 grant program to help businesses that have taken a financial hit because of the road closure."I saw them pulling out all the yellow tape around the property, so that gave me a great sign that we're moving and we're having some progress towards moving to opening again," said Eddie Rivera, owner of Señor Lechon restaurant.Rivera said his Puerto Rican restaurant opened along Military Trail about three months ago. It has now been closed for more than a week following the crash.The closure has been particularly difficult for a business with 15 employees and bills that did not stop when customers could no longer get through."Financially wise, it's been a pretty economical impact, considering we've got 15 employees and we've got a lot of businesses in the area," Rivera said.Add on the lost sales, customers, food waste, rent and payroll continuing to add up."Anything helps at this point, especially if it comes to payroll because we've got 15 employees trying to survive as well and help out as much as we can personally, but if we can have the county do some sort of grant program or maybe talk to the state or maybe talk to some at federal level that they can have some sort of help with us, that'll be great," Rivera said.Now, Palm Beach County is preparing to offer some of that help.The county's proposed Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program would set aside $250,000 in Ad Valorem funds for eligible businesses affected by the incident and the associated Military Trail closure. Businesses could receive up to $5,000, depending on eligibility, available funding and the county's calculation of each award.Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said the program was created after businesses began reaching out about the financial strain caused by the closure."We've been receiving hundreds of calls about when are we gonna reopen. You know, we have employees, we have people that need to get paid that are not getting paid," Flores said. "We need to be able to cover our own rent, and a lot of these are small businesses. These are mom-and-pop shops, and we wanna make sure that we take care of them."For businesses like Rivera's, even that amount could make a meaningful difference."Absolutely. That at least helps out for half of the payroll so we can get, you know, at least help them go on because I've got employees that got bills to pay as well," Rivera said.Businesses will have to apply through the County's Housing and Economic Development Department.The money can be used for expenses including rent or mortgage payments, employee payroll, utilities, essential inventory and supplies and other approved operating costs. Only one award is allowed per legal business as they take steps to return to normalcy.The county’s proposed $250,000 business grant program is not the only financial assistance being brought into the recovery effort. In some areas of South Florida and the Treasure Coast, the flooding from last week's heavy rains persists."It's been a definite challenge," says Jesse Cabral in the Grand Isles condos, located off Haverhill Road in West Palm Beach.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The water around his condo is still over ankle-deep and laps up to his garage."It didn’t come into the unit itself, but it did flood my garage and did do a lot of damage in there," Cabral said.For some homeowners, flood damage can lead to a break on property taxes."Under Florida law, homeowners whose residences are uninhabitable for at least 30 consecutive days due to a catastrophic event may qualify for a partial property tax refund," according to an email from Palm Beach County Appraiser Dorothy Jacks.Homeowners seeking a refund for damage must submit an Application for Catastrophic Event Tax Refund (Form DR-465) and supporting documentation by March 1, 2027.Damage sustained during this flooding will not change a property's 2026 assessment but may affect its 2027 assessment if repairs remain incomplete as of Jan. 1, 2027.Having flood insurance is still the best protection from sudden flooding events, even in areas not known for flooding in the past."This isn't a designated flood zone, and I didn't get flood insurance, so it might be a problem," Cabral said.

Eight days after the rain stopped, neighbors in a West Palm Beach community remain flooded, and they say they are not getting the answers they need to get their lives back on track.In communities like Hamilton Bay, located off of Jog Road, people know they need help a week after record rainfall moved out. But they say their requests are falling on deaf ears. So I set out to answer one of their biggest questions: Who is accountable for providing that help?WATCH REPORT BELOW: "I don't know if — who's responsible, the HOA, the city," Juliet Bradford said as she drove a rented Jeep through floodwaters. She told me her car had been totaled in those same floodwaters."It's unacceptable," Bradford said.Jackie Copan, standing on the dry upper portion of her driveway, said she hadn't left her home since last Tuesday, when she waded through floodwaters to vote."We brought a stick in case we saw a gator," Copan noted.By Monday, the water had somewhat subsided in Hamilton Bay since last week. But the frustration among neighbors has not.Sal Pahzoor said at one point, water had gotten into his garage, where he now stores the inflatable canoe and life vests he bought last week."The water has been mixed with the sewage. I saw several snakes in the water," Pahzoor said.Robin Williams described a week without basic city services."Since Halloween we've not received mail. We've not had garbage pickup. We've not had bulk pick up all week long," Williams said. "We are very disappointed about this. I know I am.""I've been living in West Palm Beach for 30 years. First time I've seen something like this," Pahzoor said.To find answers, I got on the phone, connecting with officials at Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, Hamilton Bay's property management company, and the Hamal Community Development District — which includes several flooded neighborhoods off of Okeechobee Boulevard.Dwayne Barrett, Hamal's operations manager, told me the district has been working with the county and the city, and is currently pumping water into a canal that the county allowed them to use."This is at least 16 inches (deep) right here," Pahzoor said as he drove his SUV around his neighborhood.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James sent the following statement Monday afternoon:“I understand the frustration and hardship that residents of Briar Bay, The Cove at Briar Bay, and Hamilton Bay continue to experience following last week's historic rainfall. With significant standing water remaining in these communities, the City is focused on residents’ safety and is continuing to coordinate with the agencies responsible for drainage while providing direct assistance where possible.The Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the community’s surface water management system. Its existing system has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. The Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District (NPBCID) has provided two additional pumps, and Hamal CDD informed the City this morning that an electrician is being brought in to enable its two pumps to operate concurrently.Since the beginning of this event, the City has maintained ongoing communication with the NPBCID and has also made direct outreach to Hamal CDD, offering personnel, equipment, and technical assistance. Both districts have informed us that there is nothing further the City can do at this time to assist with drainage operations. The City is not withholding permits, delaying improvements on the current pumping and drainage efforts. We will continue monitoring conditions, coordinating with the responsible agencies and offering assistance as needs change.While the drainage system is outside our jurisdiction, our commitment to these residents is not. The City partially activated its Emergency Operations Center on November 2. Since then, City crews have been working around the clock to respond to flooding throughout West Palm Beach, while continuing to provide direct assistance to residents in these communities. This includes offering transportation to shelters for residents unable to leave their neighborhoods and helping hospice nurses reach patients when they were flooded in. Our Police and Fire Rescue personnel remain available to assist residents with medical emergencies or other urgent needs, including assistance leaving their communities. Residents facing an immediate emergency should call 911.Our sanitation crews have continued assessing conditions in these neighborhoods twice daily. Due to significant standing water, garbage trucks cannot safely access certain areas without creating wakes that could push water into homes and garages. To provide residents with an alternative, the City is placing two temporary six-cubic-yard dumpsters in the community clubhouse parking lot for excess bagged household garbage. The City will continue monitoring conditions and resume regular collection as soon as it is safe to do so.I recognize the significant impact this prolonged flooding has had on residents. The City will continue coordinating with the responsible agencies, monitoring conditions, and providing assistance wherever possible. Our priority remains the safety and well-being of every resident.” For questions regarding drainage operations and floodwater removal, residents should contact the Hamal Community Development District:District Manager: Jamie OteroPhone: (561) 571-0010Email: info@hamalcdd.comWebsite: https://hamalcdd.com/contactResidents experiencing a medical emergency should call 911. City emergency services remain available to assist residents in the impacted communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For months, WPTV has been seeking answers for residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth after they reached out to me about a collapsing section of road that serves as the only way in and out of their neighborhood.Now, neighbors are finally seeing action.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV traffic reporter Johann Hoffend first connected with residents in August, when they told me the deteriorating road was getting worse and they feared it could eventually become impassable."Hopefully with the help from WPTV Channel 5, we're getting some action," one resident said. "I think they're gonna do something about it."Another neighbor described how difficult navigating the damaged section had become."This is nonsense. I can't drive one of my cars out because it bottoms out trying to go through this," the resident said.Neighbors told me repairs had been made before, but the problem kept returning."Every time they come out here, they do a little fixing, but it doesn’t take long for it to keep going down," another resident said.After recent heavy rains, I returned to Brooklyn Lane and found the hole had grown larger and deeper. Residents believed the bigger problem was underground and involved a drainage pipe beneath the roadway.Within 24 hours of my visit, the road was patched, and the pipe underneath was being assessed.Now, the county has taken the repair a step further.Crews removed water from the pipe and filled a section beneath the roadway with concrete, addressing the area below the surface rather than simply placing another patch over the damaged road.For neighbors who say they have dealt with the problem for years, the latest work represents progress.Now, they're hoping the repair beneath Brooklyn Lane will finally provide the long-term solution they've been waiting for.WPTV traffic reporter Johann Hoffend will continue following the repairs and whether they hold up over time.

A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence.The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County’s Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities.WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent livingSome of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support.Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life.During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu.From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking.Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient."We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted," said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes.Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference."Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow," Kelson said.By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made.For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of."I'm proud of it," she said. "I am going to try this at home."Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives — one meal at a time.

By: Leilyn Torres , Samantha Roesler Posted and last updated Share Copy link Facebook Nextdoor X Threads Reddit LinkedIn Email WhatsApp Messenger Print Add WPTV as a Google Preferred Source PALM BEACH COUNTY, Fla. — Heavy delays continue on Florida's Turnpike North near Boca Raton after a crash Monday morning. The Tequesta Chili Cook-Off returns Saturday, Nov. 14, with thousands of people expected to gather for chili, live music, and a celebration of veterans, but organizers say one of the event's biggest changes this year is its move to the Seabreeze Amphitheater at Carlin Park in Jupiter.The 15th annual event runs from 2 p.m. and brings together more than 30 teams of firefighters, public safety personnel and community sponsors for an afternoon organizers describe as a combination of chili competition, entertainment and patriotism.After 14 years, the cook-off is moving to a larger location at Carlin Park.Captain David McGovern of Tequesta Fire Rescue told WPTV the venue gives the growing event more room while offering easier parking and a different atmosphere near the ocean.“Bigger, beautiful location, easier to park, and just that lovely little sea breeze coming in as well,” McGovern said.The Seabreeze Amphitheater also offers paved walkways, permanent restrooms, a permanent stage and additional space for the chili teams, entertainment and guests, according to event organizers.While chili may bring people through the gates, McGovern said honoring veterans remains at the heart of the event.“We'll have (around) 4,000 people show up on Saturday to honor our veterans, give medals to our veterans,” McGovern said. “So we say thank you for all their sacrifices and everything else.”The event includes a Veterans Award Ceremony recognizing veterans and Gold Star families, along with military flyovers and performances by pipes and drums.Organizers say 100% of the event's proceeds benefit organizations serving veterans and first responders, including Wounded Veterans Relief Fund, Operation 300, Southeast Florida Honor Flight, Warriors Renewal Coalition, and Tequesta Friends of Public Safety Inc.I have covered and judged the event in previous years, and the community surrounding the cook-off is part of its appeal. This year at the judges' table will be WPTV's Ashley Glass and Janny Rodriguez. “Everybody at the station makes fun of me because I talk about this event all year and say it's my favorite thing, but my favorite thing about it is the community comes together as one, and it's just so patriotic,” I said.More than 30 teams are expected to compete for chili bragging rights.Admission includes chili tastings as well as beverages. Beer selections will include offerings from Tequesta Brewing Co., Civil Society Brewing, and Copperpoint Brewing Co., according to organizers.The event also features live music, celebrity judges, military flyovers, pipes and drums, and other activities.Girlfriend Material and Meltdown are among the scheduled musical acts.McGovern said the packed schedule creates an experience that goes well beyond choosing a favorite bowl of chili.“One minute you're laughing, next minute you're crying, but you'll remember 4 hours of just pure patriotism,” McGovern said.That combination of community, remembrance, and celebration takes on added significance heading into the event weekend, when thousands of people are expected to gather in Jupiter not simply to judge chili, but to recognize veterans and first responders while supporting organizations that serve them.The 15th Annual Tequesta Chili Cook-Off takes place Saturday, Nov. at the Seabreeze Amphitheater at Carlin Park in Jupiter.The event is strictly for guests 21 and older and has a clear-bag policy.Tickets and additional event information are available through TequestaChiliCookOff.com.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Detroit Lions have repeated a mantra all week in the aftermath of a scary neck injury to All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell.Play like No. 46.They did that against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. Jahmyr Gibbs had a rushing touchdown, Jared Goff threw for 170 yards and the Lions beat the Dolphins 19-9 for their fourth straight victory.“The whole week was prepare and play like Jack. Kind of felt like we owed it to him. It’s all we can do,” Detroit coach Dan Campbell said, adding later: “This was hard because you want to talk about it and acknowledge it. You don’t want to brush it under the rug. The guy means too much to us. We bonded together and ultimately we found a way to win the game. It was emotional.”Jake Bates made four field goals on a day that was a bit underwhelming for Goff and the Lions' top-ranked offense, which entered averaging 29 points and 395.4 yards per game but finished with 271 yards.Goff completed 17 of 25 passes while being sacked three times as Miami's defense pressured him throughout. Goff was intercepted by rookie cornerback Chris Johnson on a tipped pass in the first quarter — just the second pick he has thrown this season.Gibbs averaged just 3.7 yards per carry, finishing with 74 yards on 20 attempts and an 8-yard rushing score that put the Lions ahead 16-6 entering the fourth. Brown had 86 yards receiving for the Lions, who are trying to keep pace in a tough NFC North.Lions players arrived at Hard Rock Stadium wearing No. 46 jerseys to honor Jack Campbell, who was placed on injured reserve this week after he was hospitalized with the neck injury suffered during last Sunday's win over Minnesota.Campbell's jersey was hanging in his locker at the stadium before the game, and some fans raised signs that read “Campbell Strong.”“That’s a tough line you stand on — this balance beam of football and life and what really matters,” edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson said. “For us to come out today and get the win with all that in our head and think about him while we’re doing it, it’s really important.”The Lions never trailed but could not pull away from the rebuilding Dolphins, who had been in four consecutive one-score games entering Sunday.Bates made kicks of 28, 33, 40 and 43 yards. His 43-yarder gave Detroit a 10-point lead with 4:28 remaining.The Lions led 9-6 with four minutes left in the third when Goff connected with Jameson Williams for a 31-yard pickup — Detroit’s longest play of the game — that set up Gibbs' touchdown run on fourth down, his 11th scrimmage TD this season.Then the Dolphins took a page out of Dan Campbell's book of aggressive play-calling, executing a fake punt that gave Miami the ball at Detroit's 18, setting up a 34-yard field goal by Zane Gonzalez.Malik Willis completed 13 of 25 passes for 128 yards and an interception while facing constant pressure from Detroit's front. Willis didn't use his legs as much as he has in previous games. He has a nagging groin injury and said after the game it “was a little tight.”The Dolphins went 0 for 3 in the red zone and failed to top 100 yards rushing for the second straight game. And despite staying within striking distance, the Dolphins had far too many self-inflicted wounds — including 11 penalties, a missed field goal and a kickoff that fell short of the landing zone.“We can’t keep saying the same things like, ‘Oh, we’ve got to get better,'” Willis said. “We've got to continue to fight to actually do it and make sure that shows up on game day.”Campbell picked up his 54th regular-season win as Detroit's coach, moving into second place alone in franchise history midway through his sixth season. Wayne Fontes is the Lions' winningest coach with 66 victories from 1988-96.Dolphins punter Bradley Pinion connected with Kaytron Allen for a 46-yard completion on Miami's fourth-quarter fake punt.“I’ll take that. It was a good job by them,” Dan Campbell said. “That certainly wasn’t on our guys. That was on me.”In the second quarter, Jack Fox lined up to punt before tossing an 11-yard pass to Tay Martin, which gave Detroit the ball at the 41.The Dolphins' defense held, though, sacking Goff on third down to force a real punt.“Why did we give up the fake punt? We've got to go look back and make sure we’re not giving anything away,” Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said. “They clearly saw something on tape that they took advantage of, just like we saw something on tape and we took advantage of it.”Dolphins: TE Will Kacmarek (quad) was injured on a low hit in the third quarter. He remained down for a couple of minutes before walking to the sideline unassisted.Lions: Travel to Germany, where they will face New England in Munich next Sunday.Dolphins: At Indianapolis next Sunday.

The Miami Dolphins went up against one of the best offenses in the league, the Detroit Lions — a big test for a Dolphins defense still trying to find a rhythm this season. Holding the line for Miami is defensive tackle Jordan Phillips, the 22-year-old from Orlando, Florida, playing close to home.This week WPTV sat down with Phillips to talk about what that opportunity means and where the defensive unit is headed in the second half of the season."It means everything to me. It's always been my dream growing up, and to work my way up to this level, do this for the team, the organization, for my family. It feels great," Phillips said.Now in his second year in the NFL, Phillips said his focus has shifted toward refining the details of his game."I mainly say just technique, you know what I'm saying? Constantly improving that and being focused and intentional every time I step on the field, just working on something to get 1% better every day," Phillips said.Phillips said building chemistry with his fellow defenders is just as important as individual improvement, pointing to the group's weekly dinners away from the facility."I mean, just continuing to get better is always important. Continue to build the brotherhood," Phillips said. "Outside of the building, we just talk about personal lives and, you know, try to get to know each other better. That way, when we get on the field, that brotherhood is just natural."He credited head coach Jeff Hafley for believing in the group while pushing the players to improve."Hafley is amazing. He's a guy who believes in us, while also pushing us every day," Phillips said.Hafley had high praise for Phillips this week, calling him one of the team's unsung heroes."I love Jordan Phillips. Every time you guys bring him up, I just, those are the unsung heroes. Those are the guys that don't get credit,” Hafley said.Coach Hafley mentioned how he showed a couple clips of Phillips during this week's team meeting.“When you watch him in a walkthrough, it almost looks full speed, and he's so locked in, and he's so detailed. And then it translates to how he plays and how much he cares and the effort that he puts in and how violent he is,” Hafley said.He goes on to credit Phillips’ consistency in both practice and game time.“He's just consistent from the time he walks into this building to the time he leaves, and he's embraced his role, right? He's the type of guy that when he knows it's third and seven, he turns and, like, jogs off the field. Most guys would be pouty because what do they want to do on third and seven? This guy understands his role. He embraces his role, and I can't say enough good things about him,” Hafley said.“There is room for improvement, certainly. Would I love to see him in the pass rush continue to grow? Would I love to see him get a sack? Yeah, I can't imagine what his celebration would be like, but I'm hoping that we get to see that in the second half of the season.”Phillips said he embraces that feedback and continues to build on it.“Yeah, I mean, I get it from him and just learning the process and just continuing to build on that and trying to get better at it each and every day,” Phillips said.As for the sack his coach is hoping to see, Phillips said it would be a boost for the entire defense.“That would mean everything to me to get a sack. Not only would that help out the defense, but that'll just build momentum going forward,” Phillips said.

Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up.“So we're basically trying to track our trash,” Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. “So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them.”The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface.“Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach is balancing four community efforts this week, from responding to people displaced by a plane crash and flooding to opening an interactive museum designed to help people better understand poverty.Ellen T. Wayne, CEO of Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach, said the organization has been working with people affected by two emergencies while preparing to welcome the public to the People of Hope Mobile Museum and its “Spare Change, Share Hope” campaign.WATCH REPORT BELOW: “We got hit with a double whammy,” Wayne said. “First, we're responding to the individuals who have been displaced as a result of the plane crash here in Palm Beach County, and then, now we're in full disaster response mode working with individuals who've been impacted by this [recent] flooding that we've had across our five counties in our diocese.”The first two efforts involve Catholic Charities' response to immediate needs in the community.Wayne said the organization has been assisting people displaced by the Palm Beach County plane crash.At the same time, Catholic Charities has moved into disaster response following flooding across the five-county area served by the Diocese of Palm Beach (Okeechobee, Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Palm Beach counties).Those efforts are an extension of the organization's everyday work with people experiencing vulnerable situations, Wayne said.The third effort brings a different kind of assistance to the community: understanding.The People of Hope Mobile Museum is a traveling interactive museum housed inside an expandable semi-truck. It is visiting Catholic Charities agencies across the United States and is making a stop at the Cathedral of St. Ignatius Loyola in Palm Beach Gardens.Wayne said the experience is intended to give visitors a glimpse into the lives of people dealing with poverty while sharing stories of resilience, perseverance, and hope.Visitors can experience an interactive simulator that explores situations faced by people living in poverty, record their own stories, and leave messages of hope for others.The museum also explores circumstances faced by seniors, people experiencing homelessness, and other people Catholic Charities serves.“Oftentimes, people, when they're hearing a story of an individual struggling, will think, ‘Well, why did they do that or why didn't they do something else?’” Wayne said. “This is really going to give our guests an opportunity to see the challenges and the decisions that people have to make every day and the reality that there's no easy way out.”The pop-up museum is free to attend Friday and Saturday.The fourth effort happening this weekend is the "Spare Change. Share Hope." campaign.Visitors who want to support Catholic Charities can contribute through a QR code associated with the campaign.The campaign complements the museum's larger message by giving visitors an opportunity to move from learning about challenges their neighbors face to helping people in need.Wayne described that connection by saying Catholic Charities has “people out in the field doing the work of Hope,” while the museum gives others an opportunity to learn what it means to become a person of hope themselves.The timing gives the People of Hope Museum added relevance in Palm Beach County.While Catholic Charities responds to people affected by emergencies, the museum asks visitors to consider the difficult decisions people can face when circumstances suddenly change.“It's always easier to be on the outside looking in,” Wayne said. “This is intended to kind of open our eyes to what the struggles of people who are impoverished all across our country are facing.”The People of Hope Mobile Museum is at the Cathedral of St. Military Trail in Palm Beach Gardens.It is open Friday from 8:30 a.m. and Saturday from 8:30 a.m. Admission is free.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. While many families are dealing with flooded streets and damaged homes, some families are facing another challenge. The recent flooding is preventing them from laying their loved ones to rest. At Washington Memorial Cemetery in Jensen Beach, burials are on hold. The water is also inching closer to some of the caskets buried there, and families worry that if the ground becomes too saturated, the caskets could shift or float away. Henrietta Cooper said she visited the cemetery and was stunned by what she saw. I came this way yesterday," she said. "I looked at it and said, 'Wow.' It's unbelievable. Cooper had planned to bury her brother, Henry, at Washington Memorial Cemetery over the weekend, alongside other family members. But floodwaters put those plans on hold. I may have to find some other place to put him but all our family's here," Cooper said. "I would like for him to be here. Burial delays aren’t the only problem. See also: Cockpit voice recorder recovered as Greenacres residents return home after Learjet crash Allecia Dixon, a volunteer at the historic cemetery, which her family manages, said one casket has started sinking. Dixon said the family fears more flooding could cause caskets to float. Our fear, potentially, is that if we have more flooding that we're going to have floating caskets, she said. She said it has happened once before. Now, at least three graves are at risk after a neighborhood pond that butts up against the cemetery grounds overflowed onto the property during last week’s heavy rain. Dixon said the flooding could add to families’ grief. Families, who are trying to have closure from losing loved ones, to relive, now I have to go back and rebury my loved one in a different spot because of the level of water. That’s not healthy, said Dixon. For Cooper, the wait continues. I can't wait too long," Cooper said. CBS12 News reached out to county commissioners to find out whether there is anything the county can do to help the families. CBS12 is waiting to hear back. Meantime, relief could soon be on the way for communities hit hard by historic flooding. Ron DeSantis has requested a major disaster declaration to help secure federal funding for Central and South Florida.

The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway.Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad.Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7."At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff.However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County.Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward.WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

A week after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still facing several feet of standing water inside their homes, forcing evacuations and raising concerns about recovery. Lisa French, a resident of Skyline Heights, described how the flooding progressed since last week. "Tuesday you can kind of see the water creep towards the house, and then we started having water come out of our toilets and our showers, so we decided to leave. Wednesday, we got back here, and there’s flooding inside the house, and this all came," French said. The affected neighborhood is located near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water naturally flows south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. French said officials explained that flooding in her area is caused by water being pumped into the Savannas Preserve from Port St. "We're at level with the Savannas, so if they try to pump, it's like how they explain it is they, they're pumping us and the Savannas at the same time," French said. Lucie, they can dump all their water from their streets into the Savanna Preserve, and it's going to come down to us." French said no one in her neighborhood, including herself, had flood insurance because the area is not designated as a flood zone. As the days went on, her home became inundated with water, and now fecal matter is floating around the house, creating strong odors. "It's like a total teardown; we had people come, and everything in there has been sewer water sitting in hot heat," French said. "Right now, it’s like a hot box because there’s sewer water 4-6 inches high everywhere. My floors are up… my husband was cutting out the walls to see how far the moisture got up. It’s gross inside; we can’t go inside anymore." Martin County officials said crews are working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. On Sunday, frustrated Jensen Beach residents brought their concerns directly to county leaders. District 1 County Commissioner Eileen Vargas said, "Habitat for Humanity is working with United Way right now for a shelter... plus other help." Jim Gorton, Martin County Public Works, added, "We are working on temporary housing... Make sure you have your contact information out there; next week is tomorrow. So that's being worked on." French said while emergency services, resources, and local and federal leaders are reaching out to help her family, she hopes to rebuild her home and return to normalcy. "The first thing you think of is Thanksgiving is coming up; we’re supposed to host Thanksgiving. Then I’m supposed to do Christmas for my boys, and we don’t have a home… It’s just hard," French said. "A lot of these neighbors have become our family, like our close family, and my goal is to keep this property and live on this property. Make sure this doesn't happen again."

Florida Highway Patrol is investigating a fatal crash that occurred in Indian River County Monday afternoon. FHP says that at around 3:43 p.m. on Monday, a 2018 Toyota Rav 4 SUV and a 2017 Harley Davidson Electra Guide Motorcycle collided near 1850 37th Street within unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP , the driver of the Rav 4 SUV an 82-year-old female was traveling east on 37th Street before coming to a stop in the roadway and waiting to turn left into Indian River MRI. At the same time, the driver of the Harley Davidson a 58-year-old male was traveling west before colliding with the SUV, who turned into the path of the motorcycle as it approached. See also: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops The 82-year-old woman came away with minor injuries, while the 58-year-old male on the motorcycle was pronounced dead after being transported HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. As a result, Westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue is currently closed. This remains an active investigation.

As many communities on the Treasure Coast dry out from last week’s historic flooding, some remain underwater and residents are desperate for help. One of those communities is Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach. Related: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall It’s been a week since many who live on Hyline Drive have been able to access their homes; the water is just not budging and is now mixed in with sewage. But help is now on the way. Sandra Elliott Swann and her husband hit the road right after voting on Election Day in Pennsylvania for a quick vacation at their second home on Hyline Drive, but they haven’t been able to get there yet because of all the standing water. “We got a phone call that our house was underwater, and we kept saying. But we have storm doors and windows. And they said, it's in there. And they were trying to break it to us gently,” Sandra Elliott Swann said. Swann said they estimate there’s three feet of water in the entire house. “So everything's going to be ruined,” Swann said. Sunday, only WPBF 25’s cameras were there when residents expressed their frustration to county leaders about the flooding at a public meeting. And Monday, crews were setting up hoses on Jensen Beach Boulevard to begin the process of pumping water out of the Hyline Pond. Related: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall “We've deployed two additional pumps up to that area. And what we're doing is pumping out the receiving pond, because we have to move the water from the Hyline area to another pond and then drain it out of that pond,” Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said. It’s a process Gorton said could take at least a week or longer. “It’s going to involve a couple of things: how fast the system recovers. And we won't know that until we do it the first time. After the first time we pump, we will know our recovery rate in that pond,” Gorton said. The Swanns are glad to see crews manning the pump hoses and hoping that some progress is made before they head back up north for Thanksgiving. “I feel like they finally heard us because we've been trying since we got here with the neighbors to try to get notice that we were in trouble. And the longer that dirty water sits in our house, the worse it's going to be,” Swann said. In the coming days, Martin County officials plan to open a multi-agency resource center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach where residents affected by the flooding can get the help they need.
