cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to open applications Thursday for $1 million in flood-repair aid
cards.teaser: Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through loans forgiven over five years. Pre-applications open at 8 a.m. Thursday.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie will open pre-applications at 8 a.m. Thursday for its $1 million Disaster Relief Program, which helps low- and moderate-income homeowners repair primary residences damaged by this week's flooding. The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000, and the program will remain open until the funding is exhausted.

The assistance comes through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. It is offered as a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines. Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on mortgage and property tax payments.

According to the city, the money can pay for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses may include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. Other reasonable and necessary actions to protect the home from additional damage may also qualify. All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

The program excludes mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation. Homeowners whose properties require mold remediation must complete that work before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.

Residents can apply through the city's housing website. Homeowners who need help can contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie allocates $1 million for flood repairs; pre-applications open Thursday
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie has allocated $1 million to help eligible homeowners repair damage from this week's flooding, with pre-applications opening at 8 a.m. Thursday. The city's Disaster Relief Program offers up to $25,000 per eligible homeowner for critical repairs to primary residences. Assistance is limited to low- and moderate-income homeowners and will remain available only until the $1 million allocation is exhausted.

The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Assistance is offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Homeowners can receive a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years under program guidelines.

Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less. Homeowners also must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments.

The money may cover emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal needed to restore habitability, payment of homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. Other reasonable and necessary actions to protect the home from additional damage may also qualify. All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

The program excludes mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation. Homeowners whose properties require mold remediation must complete that work before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.

Residents can submit pre-applications through the city's housing website beginning Thursday morning. Homeowners seeking help can contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

cards.headline: David Jolly wins St. Lucie County as turnout rises despite flooding
cards.teaser: Democrat David Jolly received approximately 51% of the county’s vote for governor. Turnout exceeded the 2022 rate despite flooding that forced polling place relocations.
cards.body:
Democrat David Jolly won St. Lucie County in Tuesday’s governor’s race, carrying approximately 51% of the vote to Republican Byron Donalds’ 48% as turnout rose despite flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority of the county’s vote. Former President Barack Obama carried St. Lucie County with 53.42% that year. Jolly’s county victory came as election officials moved several voting locations because of flooding across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce.

Voter turnout reached 56.5%, an increase of 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election, when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. In that election, 122,361 of St. Lucie County’s 238,645 registered voters voted. The county ranked 51st among Florida’s 67 counties, with 16 counties reporting lower turnout. Tuesday’s participation exceeded the county’s previous gubernatorial election turnout rate even as flooding disrupted access to some polling locations and required voters to cast ballots at alternate sites.

St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the polling place changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected by the relocations. Some voters were redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes affected several polling places across the three communities as election officials responded to the flooding.

Heavy rainfall submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of St. Lucie County. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for the county and six other Florida counties. Flooding also forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Those conditions coincided with Election Day, when the county recorded both a higher turnout rate than in 2022 and a Democratic majority in the governor’s race.

hero.headline: Florida special session expected to implement Amendment 3 homestead tax relief
hero.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that a special legislative session is expected to implement Amendment 3, the voter-approved measure expanding homestead property tax relief. The amendment must be implemented by Jan. 1. DeSantis said the legislation would set a schedule for further relief and seek to prevent local governments from offsetting homeowners’ savings with other taxes or fees.

DeSantis said he would work with legislative leaders to determine when lawmakers should return to Tallahassee before he leaves office in January. He wants lawmakers to establish what he called a “taxpayer bill of rights” and is considering state grants to help local governments cover essential services. That assistance could total tens of millions of dollars, particularly for rural communities facing funding shortfalls for core services such as sheriff’s departments, he said. “It's not going to be a tax shift,” DeSantis said. “It's going to be a reduction.”

Amendment 3 does not apply to school districts, and DeSantis said the implementing legislation would preserve that exemption. He suggested lawmakers could eventually revisit Florida’s education funding formula as they consider additional property tax relief for homeowners without reducing support for public schools. His ultimate goal is to move Florida closer to making homesteaded property tax-free, though he said that would require additional action after his term ends. “The more we can get the homestead to just be tax free, I think that's the better,” he said.

Speaking the day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, DeSantis also credited Amendment 3 with helping Republicans withstand major Democratic gains elsewhere in the country. He argued that the measure drew voters who then supported Republican candidates further down the ballot. “Had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot, I don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out,” he said.

DeSantis described the national results as “close to an extinction-level event” for Republicans but said Florida’s results reflected voter trust in the party’s record during his two terms. cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls
cards.body:
Emergency crews handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding in St. Lucie County, officials said Tuesday, as rescue operations continued and the county opened two shelters. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and warned that floodwater could take several days to recede.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said crews received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period. County public safety director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, areas around California and Peacock boulevards, and areas around Virginia Avenue. The Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews were assessing roads and infrastructure. They were also clearing drainage and roadways, though safety concerns limited some high-water operations after dark.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, and the landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations.

Officials warned that road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents seeking relocated vehicles can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with pickups shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should discard food or household items exposed to floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes in Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.body:
Steven Giordano unseated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and increasing transparency in city spending.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin’s 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail votes were marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m.

During his campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share of infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion and sought to hold developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. He also called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration’s approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for a growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. Martin also pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city’s property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August’s three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The latest election results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County moving flood shelters as Port St. Lucie flooding persists
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its temporary flood shelters Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen, while significant standing water remains in parts of Port St. Lucie. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede as recovery efforts continue.

The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter is relocating from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts and working to restore normal conditions safely.

Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano defeats Shannon Martin to win Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.teaser: Giordano won by just over 2,400 votes, reversing a nearly 13-percentage-point deficit to Martin in the August primary.
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Shannon Martin by just over 2,400 votes to win the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, reversing his nearly 13-percentage-point deficit in the August primary.

Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. At his election-night watch party, he said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race.

“I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons,” Giordano said. “I think they watched the debate.”

Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. “I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people,” he said. “And I'm proud to be the people's mayor.”

The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water calls; schools closed Wednesday
cards.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, officials said Tuesday. Schools were set to remain closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Officials warned that road conditions could change quickly and urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said water could take several days to recede.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. Residents should call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said dispatchers received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Call takers were screening requests to keep emergency vehicles available for urgent situations.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service over 36 hours. Guerrero estimated rainfall totals at 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area and Tradition, along with neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive. Areas around California Boulevard, Peacock Boulevard and Virginia Avenue also flooded.

The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews continued high-water rescues, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Guerrero said safety concerns limited some high-water operations after dark. The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions.

Port St. Lucie residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with service shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that touched floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes. Questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can be directed to 772-873-4931.

hero.headline: Flood-related polling relocations extend beyond Precinct 90 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Flood-related Election Day polling changes in St. Lucie County extend beyond the relocation of Precinct 90 from Legacy High School to Tradition Town Hall. Election officials also designated replacement voting sites for precincts 49, 71, 51, 67, 86, 83, 92 and 12, with specific access routes for two locations.

The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves were intended to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots.

The notice directs voters in precincts 49 and 71, whose regular polling place is Oak Hammock K-8 School, to the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, are also assigned to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard.

For precincts 67 and 86, the replacement polling place is Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd., replacing Centennial High School. The county designates Peacock Boulevard as the access route.

In the Tradition area, Precinct 83 voters are directed from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters, whose regular polling place is The Brennity at Tradition, are also assigned to Tradition Town Hall. That facility is also the replacement site for Precinct 90, where flooding and police roadblocks disrupted access to Legacy High School. The Precinct 90 relocation replaced earlier instructions to reach the school by an alternate route.

In Fort Pierce, the notice directs Precinct 12 voters from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1.

Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin as Port St. Lucie mayor by 2,601 votes
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail voting results were marked complete as of 12:34 a.m.

Throughout the campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share for infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion. On city spending, Giordano called for an independent forensic audit and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. On taxpayer spending, Martin cited 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The nonbinding referendum provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools closed Wednesday as flood recovery could take seven days
cards.teaser: The county opened a shelter at Northport K-8 School as crews responded to flooding. Officials urged residents to stay home if possible and reserve 911 for life-threatening emergencies.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County schools are closed Wednesday after flooding disrupted road access and left students walking through standing water to get home Monday. County leaders warned that conditions could take up to seven days to return to normal as emergency crews continued their flood response.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the district expects to reopen schools Thursday if roads are clear. During a Tuesday news conference, he apologized to families for the stress caused by Monday’s conditions and said the district had not anticipated the extent of the flooding.

The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals and coffee. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials asked residents to stay home if they can and call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

In the Tradition area, a private security company that patrols homeowners associations joined rescue efforts with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. Matchton said the crews set out to help people wherever they could with the resources they had.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods. He warned that anyone who preys on flood victims would face zero tolerance. Del Toro emphasized that responders were working together to serve the community.

Flooding also forced Election Day polling-place changes. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to voting sites. The changes included moving voting from Oak Hammock K-8 School and the Disabled American Veterans Hall to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, and from the Paula A. Lewis Library and The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce restaurant owner promotes free books, renovates space for reading room
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is helping children get books mailed to their homes through New Worlds Reading while turning part of his restaurant into a reading room.
cards.body:
FORT PIERCE, Fla. Scott Van Duzer, owner of Big Apple Pizza, is working to connect children with free books mailed to their homes while renovating part of his restaurant into a reading room. He wants to expand access to books for children, especially those from low-income families.

Van Duzer has been involved with Read To Succeed, which he said has distributed 40,000 books over three years. He is now promoting New Worlds Reading as a way to get books to children more quickly. Van Duzer said signing up takes less than five minutes and children receive nine free books a year through fifth grade.

Amy York and her son Tripp read together using books he receives through New Worlds Reading. York described the program as a partnership with the University of Florida and Scholastic. “Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house,” York said.

The reading room renovation is another part of Van Duzer’s effort to help children improve their reading. He emphasized the importance of giving children access to books early and keeping books in their homes. “It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home,” he said.

lead_independence.lead: St. Lucie County schools are closed Wednesday after flooding disrupted road access and left students walking through standing water to get home Monday.
